Three years ago I shipped a pricing change on a Friday afternoon and took down checkout for 40 minutes. We lost about $12k in orders and I spent the weekend writing the post-mortem. The fix wasn't technical — we added a rule that no pricing change goes out after noon on a Friday. Boring, unglamorous, and we haven't had a weekend outage since. The best reliability work rarely looks impressive.

I used to think onboarding was a checklist. Then I watched our Q1 cohort: the 6 new hires who paired with someone on day one shipped their first PR in 4 days; the 5 who didn't took 11. Same docs, same tooling. The variable was a human who answered the dumb questions in real time. We now assign a day-one buddy to everyone — it's the cheapest retention lever we've found.

Spent last Tuesday rewriting our incident template. Cut it from 9 sections to 3: what broke, who it hit, what we changed. Adoption went from 'nobody fills it out' to every incident this week. Shorter forms get filled.
Everyone talks about crypto, but let's talk about mindset. Winners never quit and quitters never win. Hustle harder, dream bigger, and manifest your best life. The only limit is you. Who's with me?

Last March a client had 11 days of cash and didn't know it. Their forecast was built on invoice dates, not when customers actually paid. We rebuilt it on 90 days of real bank receipts in an afternoon. The gap was 19 days. They raised a bridge two weeks earlier than they would have. Forecast on receipts, not invoices.

Second shift kept scrapping 6% more castings than first. Same die, same alloy. Turned out the second-shift lead topped up the holding furnace an hour later, so metal ran 15 degrees cooler for the first pours. We moved the top-up. Scrap matched within a week. The fix was a clock, not a sensor.

We lost 9 of 20 new warehouse hires in their first month last year. Exit calls all said the same thing: first day they were handed a scanner and a quota. This year week one is shadow-only, no quota. We've lost 2 of 22. I wish I'd asked them sooner.

Our first 30 discovery calls were useless because I kept pitching. Call 31 I only asked how they scheduled jobs on a bad day. The dispatcher talked for 40 minutes. That call wrote our roadmap for the next six months.

The night I almost missed a sepsis case wasn't about skill. It was the fourth admission in an hour and the vitals were on a clipboard at the other end of the hall. We moved the clipboard. Small things carry patients.

El año pasado perdimos a nuestro mejor cliente por una entrega mal coordinada. No fue la herramienta, fue la falta de una llamada de diez minutos los viernes. Desde entonces, no nos saltamos esa llamada.

Six months ago our hospital's discharge process averaged 4.2 hours from physician order to the patient leaving the floor. Everyone blamed transport. When we actually walked the process with a stopwatch, transport was 20 minutes of it. The rest was waiting: pharmacy reconciliation queued behind morning rounds, discharge paperwork printed at a nurses' station on another floor, and family pickup that nobody called until the order was signed. We changed three things. Pharmacy started reconciling likely discharges the evening before. We moved the printer. And the unit clerk now calls the family the moment the physician says 'probably tomorrow', not when the order lands. Average is now 2.1 hours. None of it needed new software. The hardest part was getting people to stop defending the old process long enough to time it. If you run a unit, time one discharge end to end this week.
